title: Inference-Based RC Questions
tagline: Year 3 — Questions that ask what a passage implies, assumes or supports rather than what it says

introduction.overview: An inference question asks for something the passage does not say outright but makes very likely. The answer is never new information; it is a short logical step from what the passage says. This chapter teaches the rules of safe inference: stay close to the text, prefer the modest option to the dramatic one, use numbers and cause-and-effect links, and check that denying your answer would make the passage inconsistent.
introduction.placementRelevance: Inference questions form the largest share of questions in advanced reading-comprehension sets.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading between the lines of an email or a news report without over-claiming is the same skill.

learningObjectives: Separate a safe inference from a guess
Use numbers in a passage to draw inferences
Reject extreme, absolute or out-of-scope options

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: An inference is supported by the passage; a guess is merely consistent with it.

coreDefinitions: Safe inference: follows from the passage with little or no extra assumption.
Denial test: if denying the option makes the passage inconsistent, the option is a safe inference.
Extreme option: uses always, never, all, only, completely, which the passage rarely supports.
Scope: the topic and limits of the passage. Options outside the scope are wrong.
Implication: what the passage suggests by what it says and how it says it.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: An inference is the answer to the question "what must also be true if this passage is true?" Anything beyond that is a guess.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Restate the passage in one sentence, then ask which option must be true. If an option needs an extra assumption, prefer another one that needs none.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Denial test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Deny the option; does the passage break?

mainNarrative: The library closed on Sundays and weekday attendance fell by a third, although fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The survey measured Sunday use, but not the effect of Sunday habits on other days. A safe inference is that closing on Sundays affected weekday use in a way the earlier survey did not predict.

In the restaurant passage, customers did not leave when the price doubled and profits rose. The owner says her customers were office workers whose employers paid for lunch. It follows that the customers were not sensitive to the price, not that they liked the food more.

Numbers need comparison. Accidents rose from 400 to 480, but the number of cyclists doubled from 20,000 to 40,000. Accidents per 1,000 cyclists fell from 20 to 12. The analyst's point is that the rate of accidents per cyclist fell, so the mayor's conclusion does not follow.
Use the denial test. If you deny "the accident rate fell", the analyst's remark would collapse; if you deny "cycling lanes are perfect", nothing in the passage changes, so it is not an inference.
Avoid extremes. "All cyclists are safer" or "lanes have eliminated accidents" go beyond what the numbers show.

deepDiveAspects.title: Rates and totals
deepDiveAspects.content: A rise in the total can accompany a fall in the rate when the base grows faster.

deepDiveAspects.title: Mechanism language
deepDiveAspects.content: Phrases like "therefore" and "because" are signals that a stated cause is part of what can be inferred.

solvedExamples.title: Rate inference
solvedExamples.question: Accidents rose from 400 to 480 while cyclists doubled from 20,000 to 40,000. What can be inferred about accidents per 1,000 cyclists?

solvedExamples.title: Mechanism
solvedExamples.question: The restaurant's customers kept coming when the price doubled because their employers paid for lunch. What can be inferred about these customers?

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.explanation: The customers do not bear the cost.

steps.title: Inference
steps.explanation: They are not sensitive to the price.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: They were not very sensitive to the price of the lunch
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It does not say they liked the food more.

solvedExamples.title: Denial test
solvedExamples.question: The library lost a third of its weekday evening attendance after closing on Sundays. Is "the closure affected weekday attendance" a safe inference?
givenInfo: Timing and size of the drop

steps.title: Deny
steps.explanation: If the closure did not affect attendance, the drop would be unexplained, and the librarian's suggestion would be pointless.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Yes, it is a safe inference

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Restate the passage, then pick the option that must be true and that needs no extra assumption; use the denial test to confirm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a plausible but unsupported option

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options with always, never, all or only unless the passage uses them.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Restate the passage in one sentence before reading the options.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The correct answer is usually the least dramatic.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

When the town library announced that it would close on Sundays to save money, attendance at its weekday evening sessions fell by a third within two months. Yet the library's own survey, conducted a year earlier, had shown that fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The librarian suggested that many visitors had combined a Sunday visit with a family outing and that, once that habit was broken, they had stopped coming at all.

The passage suggests that closing the library on Sundays
options: was favoured by most borrowers in the survey
affected weekday attendance in a way the earlier survey did not predict
increased the number of weekday sessions
saved the library more money than expected
easy.correctAnswer: affected weekday attendance in a way the earlier survey did not predict
easy.explanation: Weekday attendance fell by a third even though few borrowers came on Sundays, so the effect went beyond what the survey would have predicted.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

When the town library announced that it would close on Sundays to save money, attendance at its weekday evening sessions fell by a third within two months. Yet the library's own survey, conducted a year earlier, had shown that fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The librarian suggested that many visitors had combined a Sunday visit with a family outing and that, once that habit was broken, they had stopped coming at all.

Which of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
options: Sunday visits were linked with visitors' habits on other days
Fewer than one in ten borrowers disliked the library
The library had too many borrowers on Sundays
Family outings are less common on weekdays
easy.correctAnswer: Sunday visits were linked with visitors' habits on other days
easy.explanation: The librarian suggests that Sunday visits were part of a habit; breaking it reduced weekday use.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A restaurant that doubled the price of its set lunch expected its customers to leave. Instead, the number of lunch customers stayed almost the same, and the restaurant's profits rose sharply. The owner admitted that she had not understood her customers: most of them were office workers whose employers paid for lunch, and who therefore noticed the price far less than she had assumed.

The owner's statement implies that
options: the food was of poor quality
the lunch was cheaper than competitors'
she regretted raising the price
most customers did not pay for their own lunch
easy.correctAnswer: most customers did not pay for their own lunch
easy.explanation: The owner says employers paid for lunch, so most customers did not pay for it themselves.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

When the town library announced that it would close on Sundays to save money, attendance at its weekday evening sessions fell by a third within two months. Yet the library's own survey, conducted a year earlier, had shown that fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The librarian suggested that many visitors had combined a Sunday visit with a family outing and that, once that habit was broken, they had stopped coming at all.

The librarian's explanation assumes that
options: some visitors came on weekdays partly because of their Sunday library habit
the survey was inaccurate
weekday sessions are more popular than Sunday sessions
the closure was announced too late
intermediate.correctAnswer: some visitors came on weekdays partly because of their Sunday library habit
intermediate.explanation: To explain a weekday fall by the end of a Sunday habit, the librarian assumes that weekday use was partly tied to the Sunday habit.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

When the town library announced that it would close on Sundays to save money, attendance at its weekday evening sessions fell by a third within two months. Yet the library's own survey, conducted a year earlier, had shown that fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The librarian suggested that many visitors had combined a Sunday visit with a family outing and that, once that habit was broken, they had stopped coming at all.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the librarian's explanation?
options: The library's survey was conducted in summer
The library's weekday opening hours were extended
A new cinema opened in the town
Many of those who stopped coming had earlier visited on both Sundays and weekdays
intermediate.correctAnswer: Many of those who stopped coming had earlier visited on both Sundays and weekdays
intermediate.explanation: It links the lost weekday attendance to people who had a Sunday visiting habit.

intermediate.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A restaurant that doubled the price of its set lunch expected its customers to leave. Instead, the number of lunch customers stayed almost the same, and the restaurant's profits rose sharply. The owner admitted that she had not understood her customers: most of them were office workers whose employers paid for lunch, and who therefore noticed the price far less than she had assumed.

The owner's mistake was that she
options: set the price too low
ignored her competitors
reduced the quality of the lunch
misjudged how price-sensitive her customers were
intermediate.correctAnswer: misjudged how price-sensitive her customers were
intermediate.explanation: She expected customers to leave but they did not, because they were not paying; she had misjudged their price sensitivity.

advanced.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A restaurant that doubled the price of its set lunch expected its customers to leave. Instead, the number of lunch customers stayed almost the same, and the restaurant's profits rose sharply. The owner admitted that she had not understood her customers: most of them were office workers whose employers paid for lunch, and who therefore noticed the price far less than she had assumed.

If the owner raised the price again, the effect on profit would most likely depend on
options: the number of dishes on the menu
the quality of the dessert
whether customers would remain unaware of the price
the colour of the menu
advanced.correctAnswer: whether customers would remain unaware of the price
advanced.explanation: The earlier rise worked because customers barely noticed the price; a further rise would depend on whether that continued.

advanced.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A city recorded 480 cycling accidents last year, up from 400 the year before. The mayor said this showed that cycling lanes were failing. A transport analyst pointed out that the number of people cycling to work had increased from 20,000 to 40,000 over the same period, and that the number of accidents per 1,000 cyclists had therefore fallen.

Suppose cyclists had risen only to 30,000 with 480 accidents. Compared with the passage, the accident rate per 1,000 cyclists would be
options: lower
higher
the same
impossible to tell
advanced.explanation: 480 ÷ 30 = 16 per 1,000, compared with 12 in the passage, so it would be higher.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

When the town library announced that it would close on Sundays to save money, attendance at its weekday evening sessions fell by a third within two months. Yet the library's own survey, conducted a year earlier, had shown that fewer than one in ten borrowers came on Sundays. The librarian suggested that many visitors had combined a Sunday visit with a family outing and that, once that habit was broken, they had stopped coming at all.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the librarian's explanation?
options: The Sunday visitors were mostly families
The weekday sessions dropped because the council raised evening bus fares
The library reopened on Sundays later
The survey was repeated and gave the same result
placementStyle.correctAnswer: The weekday sessions dropped because the council raised evening bus fares
placementStyle.explanation: A separate cause (higher bus fares) would explain the weekday fall without the Sunday habit.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A restaurant that doubled the price of its set lunch expected its customers to leave. Instead, the number of lunch customers stayed almost the same, and the restaurant's profits rose sharply. The owner admitted that she had not understood her customers: most of them were office workers whose employers paid for lunch, and who therefore noticed the price far less than she had assumed.

Which of the following best captures the lesson of the passage?
options: Assumptions about customers should be tested against their actual behaviour
Higher prices always raise profit
Restaurants should serve lunch to office workers only
Owners should never change their prices
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Assumptions about customers should be tested against their actual behaviour
placementStyle.explanation: The owner expected one outcome and learned another from what customers actually did.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

A city recorded 480 cycling accidents last year, up from 400 the year before. The mayor said this showed that cycling lanes were failing. A transport analyst pointed out that the number of people cycling to work had increased from 20,000 to 40,000 over the same period, and that the number of accidents per 1,000 cyclists had therefore fallen.

A critic says that "total accident numbers are the only fair measure of safety". The passage most directly challenges this by
options: arguing that cycling is dangerous
comparing two cities
questioning the survey method
showing that a rate can fall while the total rises
placementStyle.correctAnswer: showing that a rate can fall while the total rises
placementStyle.explanation: The analyst uses accidents per 1,000 cyclists to show that safety can improve while the total rises.
